The Picarel (Spicara flexuosum) exhibits a life-history strategy typical of small, short-lived coastal sparids. Field surveys in the Mediterranean indicate that the maximum total length attained by this species is 23.2 cm [Li = 23.2 cm], a size considerably smaller than that of its congener Spicara maena. This ultimate length is rarely observed, with most individuals in trawl samples measuring between 15 and 20 cm, suggesting that full size is achieved only late in life. The body mass associated with this maximum length, calculated from region-specific length-weight relationships, reaches approximately 152.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 152.7 grams], a value that reflects the moderately compressed body form and relatively low condition factor of this benthic forager. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, derived from demersal eggs with a diameter of roughly 0.78 mm, have an estimated wet weight at birth of just 0.000248 grams [Wwb = 0.000248 grams], placing them among the smallest propagules in the genus. This minimal starting mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding after yolk-sac resorption.

Sexual maturation in Spicara flexuosum occurs at a notably small body size relative to its ultimate potential. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue reveal that puberty is attained at a total length of 9.1 cm [Lp = 9.1 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 9.04 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.04 grams]. Achieving this size typically requires the first year of growth, after which individuals begin a protogynous reproductive cycle in which most fish function initially as females. The onset of vitellogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis are triggered by a combination of photoperiod cues and rising water temperatures. The length-based progression to maturity is relatively tightly constrained across the population, with few individuals maturing at sizes far from this mean, a pattern that suggests strong stabilizing selection for an optimal size at first reproduction in this variable coastal environment.

Under thermal conditions characteristic of the late spring and summer spawning period in the eastern Mediterranean, approximately 14.5 °C [T = 14.5 °C], the reproductive output of Spicara flexuosum is considerable. Estimates of fecundity, scaled from the well-documented fecundity of its congener Spicara maena using a cubic relationship with body length, indicate that a female at the ultimate length can produce on average approximately 33721 eggs over the entire spawning season [Ri = approximately 33721 eggs over the entire spawning season], which corresponds to approximately 92 eggs per day when averaged over the roughly 365-day year. This high reproductive output is consistent with the species' role as a short-lived, opportunistic spawner that capitalizes on planktonic food availability for its pelagic larvae.

The complete life cycle of Spicara flexuosum is characterized by a relatively compressed timespan typical of small teleosts in warm-temperate seas. At a water temperature of 14.5 °C [T = 14.5 °C], the lifespan is documented at 4,380 days [am = 4,380 days], which corresponds to approximately twelve years, though this maximum longevity is achieved only by a small fraction of the population under ideal conditions. Mortality in the first year is exceptionally high, driven by predation on pelagic larvae and early juveniles during their transition to demersal habitats. The comparatively extended maximum lifespan, relative to body size, is somewhat unusual among Mediterranean sparids of similar ultimate length, and may reflect a combination of low adult predation risk in rocky reef refuges and a relatively slow pace of senescence in this particular lineage. Across monitored populations, survival curves show a Type III pattern, with extreme early mortality followed by a long plateau of low adult attrition.

A comparison of the size at puberty with the ultimate total length underscores the life-history prioritization of early reproduction in Spicara flexuosum. Reaching puberty at just 9.1 cm [Lp = 9.1 cm] total length against a maximum of 23.2 cm [Li = 23.2 cm] indicates that individuals invest in reproduction at less than forty percent of their ultimate length, a pattern common among protogynous species where early female function maximizes lifetime fecundity before a potential sex change. The corresponding body mass at puberty of 9.04 grams [Wwp = 9.04 grams] relative to the ultimate weight of 152.7 grams [Wwi = 152.7 grams] further emphasizes this early allocation to reproduction. The high fecundity of approximately 33721 eggs per season [Ri = approximately 33721 eggs per season] ensures that even short-lived individuals contribute significantly to the next generation, a classic trait of opportunistic, early-maturing teleosts in variable coastal ecosystems.
